concept.name: Grid trading
concept.definition: A systematic order-placement technique that lays a ladder of buy and sell orders at fixed price intervals above and below a reference price, harvesting oscillation or trend mechanically without forecasting direction. With-the-trend grids add exposure as price runs; against-the-trend (range) grids buy lower rungs and sell higher rungs to monetize mean reversion.
concept.intuition: Instead of predicting where price will go, the grid turns the price axis into a conveyor belt: each step down triggers a buy and each step back up triggers a sell at the next rung, locking the spacing in as gross profit per completed cycle.
concept.mechanics: Choose a base price, an interval (e.g., 10 pips), and a number of rungs, then place resting orders at each level. Range grids place buys below and sells above the base; trend grids do the reverse. Risk control requires a hard stop beyond the outermost rung, because position size grows against an adverse trend.
concept.formula: Gross profit per completed grid cycle approx. grid interval x size per rung; with n rungs at spacing s around base P, orders sit at P +/- k*s for k = 1..n.
concept.failure_modes: A sustained trend through the grid accumulates a large losing position (range grid) or forces profit give-back (trend grid); without a stop, a one-way move can exceed the sum of all harvested oscillation profits many times over.
concept.misconceptions: That grid trading is a low-risk money machine because it wins frequently; the many small wins are paid for with an unbounded tail loss when price leaves the grid and never returns.
concept.example: With EURUSD at 1.1450, place buys every 10 pips down to 1.1390 and sells every 10 pips up to 1.1510 with a stop at 1.1530; each completed down-up oscillation earns 10 pips per unit, while a run to 1.1530 stops the grid for a 270-pip worst case.
